title: Write an ADR for every architecturally significant decision.
Keep ADRs in the repository next to the code as numbered Markdown files, for example `docs/decisions/0001-use-postgresql.md`.
Record the options you considered and why you rejected them, not just the option you chose.
Don't rewrite accepted decisions. Supersede them with a new ADR and link the two.
Say how compliance will be confirmed, for example with a design or code review, an architecture test such as ArchUnit, or a fitness function.
Decentralise decisions with an advice process.
Treat model inputs and outputs as untrusted.
Start with the simplest solution, such as a single model call with retrieval.
Build evaluations early and run them on every change to prompts, models or tools.
Use workflows (predefined code paths) for well-defined tasks, and agents only where the model must decide the steps itself.
Design tools specifically for agents, and put as much effort into the agent interface as you would into a human one: clear, distinct names, focused scope and actionable error messages.
Treat context as a finite resource and curate what goes into it.
Budget for the hidden technical debt of ML systems: data dependencies, feedback loops and glue code.
Don't be afraid to launch without machine learning.
Use a UI layer and a data layer, and add a domain layer only when logic is complex or reused.
Keep a single source of truth for each data type, and use unidirectional data flow: state flows down, events flow up.
Expose UI state from ViewModels as observable streams, and keep UI elements free of business logic.
Access data only through repositories in the data layer.
Use dependency injection (Hilt).
Follow the coroutine best practices: inject dispatchers, make suspend functions main-safe, and don't expose mutable state.
Build offline-first where possible, with the local database as the source of truth.
Modularise by feature and layer as the app and team grow.
Make operations safe to retry, using idempotency keys where the method isn't naturally idempotent.
Evolve APIs in backward-compatible ways.
Use HTTP methods and status codes as their specification defines them.
Design the API contract first and review it before implementing it.
Model HTTP APIs around resources and standard methods, not ad-hoc RPC verbs.
Paginate list endpoints from day one.
Return machine-readable errors in the Problem Details format.
With enough users, every observable behaviour will be depended on by someone, whether documented or not (Hyrum's law).
Verify compatibility between providers and consumers with consumer-driven contract tests.
For gRPC and Protocol Buffers, follow the official dos and don'ts on field numbering and evolution.
Apply least privilege, and use temporary credentials (federation and roles) instead of long-term access keys.
Use a multi-account structure with AWS Organizations, separating workloads and environments into their own accounts.
Design for Availability Zone failure, and understand AWS fault isolation boundaries.
Define all infrastructure as code.
Review each workload against the Well-Architected Framework early in design and before go-live, and again after significant architecture changes.
Choose a disaster recovery strategy from your RTO and RPO: backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, or multi-site active/active.
Set organisation-wide guardrails with service control policies.
In Lambda functions, separate the handler from the core logic, and reuse the execution environment for clients and connections.
Tag resources consistently for ownership, cost allocation and automation.
Contain the blast radius of failures with cell-based or shuffle-sharded designs where scale demands it.
Give each service or module exclusive ownership of its data.
Evolve database schemas through small, versioned migrations kept in source control.
Keep data consistent across services with sagas, not distributed transactions.
Publish events atomically with state changes using a transactional outbox.
Choose the consistency level per use case and make eventual consistency visible in the design.
Choose storage technology per need, but count the operational cost of every extra datastore.
At organisational scale, treat analytical data as a product owned by domain teams (data mesh).
Build a ubiquitous language with domain experts and use it everywhere: in conversations, documents and code.
Split large domains into bounded contexts, each with its own model, and make the relationships between them explicit.
Spend modelling effort on the core domain; buy or simplify generic subdomains.
Use aggregates as consistency boundaries.
Put behaviour next to the data it changes and avoid anemic domain models.
Model concepts that are defined by their attributes as immutable value objects.
Start with a system context diagram and a container diagram.
Store, version and review documentation alongside the code.
Give every diagram a title, a key or legend, and labelled, directed relationships.
Keep diagrams as text in the repository so they can be reviewed and diffed.
Use the C4 abstractions (person, software system, container, component) consistently, whatever the notation.
Don't mix tutorials, how-to guides, reference and explanation in one document.
Keep secrets out of source.
Go async all the way and never block on async code with `.Result` or `.Wait()`.
Use the built-in DI container and follow its lifetime guidelines.
Add standard resilience (timeouts, retries, circuit breakers) to outgoing HTTP calls.
Structure apps with Clean Architecture.
Return errors as ProblemDetails, and handle exceptions centrally.
Expose health checks for load balancers and orchestrators.
Instrument with OpenTelemetry.
Enable nullable reference types in all projects.
Test the HTTP pipeline with in-memory integration tests (`WebApplicationFactory`), and enforce layering with architecture tests.
Bind configuration to strongly typed classes with the options pattern.
Follow the EF Core performance guidance for queries and change tracking.
Separate the UI layer (views and view models) from the data layer (repositories and services), and add a domain layer of use cases only when needed.
Make repositories the source of truth for app data, with services that wrap external APIs.
Use unidirectional data flow and immutable data models.
Cover logic with unit tests, widgets with widget tests, and critical flows with integration tests.
Choose a state management approach that fits the app and the team, and use it consistently for app state. `setState` is fine for widget-local state.
Model user actions as commands, and model operation outcomes as `Result` values instead of throwing across layers.
Advance the simulation in fixed time steps, decoupled from the render rate, and interpolate between the last two simulated states when rendering.
Build game entities by composing components, not through deep inheritance hierarchies.
Define entity types and tuning values as data that designers can change without recompiling, not as one subclass per type.
Adopt an entity component system (ECS) deliberately, when you need very large numbers of entities, and prefer an established framework to writing your own.
In competitive multiplayer games, make the server authoritative: clients send inputs, and the server runs the simulation and sends back the results.
Hide latency with client-side prediction and server reconciliation.
Render other players slightly in the past, interpolating between buffered server updates, instead of snapping to each update as it arrives.
For hit detection in fast-paced shooters, use lag compensation: the server rewinds the world to the moment the shooter saw it and checks the hit there.
Choose deterministic lockstep, which sends only inputs, only if the simulation is bit-for-bit deterministic on every platform you ship to. Otherwise, synchronise state.
Version the save-data schema from the first release, and migrate older saves to the current version when loading them.
Keep the last good save until the new one is completely written, and store an integrity check so that a corrupt or partial save falls back to the previous one.
Set a frame-time budget for each target platform (33.3 ms at 30 fps, 16.7 ms at 60 fps), and measure against it with a profiler on the target hardware, before and after each optimisation.
Pool objects that are created and destroyed often, such as projectiles and particles, instead of allocating and freeing each one.
Rearrange data for cache locality only where profiling shows that cache misses cost time.
Set the `GITHUB_TOKEN` to read-only at the top of each workflow, and grant write permissions only to the jobs that need them.
Pin third-party actions and reusable workflows to a full-length commit SHA, or lock them with a workflow dependency lockfile.
Never expand untrusted input, such as `${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}`, directly in a `run:` script. Pass it through an intermediate environment variable.
Use `pull_request` rather than `pull_request_target` unless fork pull requests need secrets or write access, and never execute pull request code in a `pull_request_target` or `workflow_run` workflow.
Authenticate to cloud providers with OpenID Connect instead of long-lived cloud secrets, and restrict the trust policy to specific repositories, branches or environments.
Avoid self-hosted runners in public repositories. Where you use them, prefer ephemeral just-in-time runners.
Enable Dependabot version updates for the `github-actions` ecosystem.
Treat restored caches as untrusted input: never cache secrets, and write caches only from workflows with trusted triggers.
Require approval from designated code owners for changes to `.github/workflows`.
Pass secrets to reusable workflows by name instead of with `secrets: inherit`.
Deploy through environments with protection rules: required reviewers, allowed deployment branches, and secrets scoped to the environment.
Share CI logic through reusable workflows (whole jobs) and composite actions (steps) instead of copying YAML between workflows and repositories.
Use concurrency groups to cancel superseded runs on the same branch and to stop deployments to the same environment from running at once.
Commit the `.import` files next to your assets and the `.uid` files next to your scripts and shaders, and ignore the `.godot/` folder.
Use snake_case for file and folder names (C# scripts excepted), and keep third-party code in `addons/`.
Design scenes to work on their own: keep what a scene needs inside it, and let the parent supply any outside dependency.
Let parents call methods on and set properties of their children, and let children report what happened through signals.
Use autoloads only for broad-scoped systems that manage their own data, such as a quest or dialogue system.
Reference other nodes through `@export` properties or scene-unique names (`%Name`), not long hard-coded node paths.
Make game-specific concepts scenes, and use named script classes for reusable tools shared across projects.
Use `RefCounted` or `Resource` classes instead of nodes for data and logic that don't need to be in the scene tree.
Use static typing throughout, and set the `untyped_declaration` warning to Error so that untyped declarations stop a script from compiling.
Follow the GDScript style guide, including its code order.
Move objects and run game logic in `_physics_process`, and turn on physics interpolation so that motion stays smooth at any frame rate.
Model designer-edited game data as custom Resource classes saved as `.tres` files.
Write saves and settings to `user://`, and don't decode objects (`allow_objects`) from files that players can edit or share.
Write automated tests with GUT or gdUnit4, and run them headless in CI on every change.
Give every container CPU and memory requests and a memory limit. Set CPU limits only where needed, for example on sensitive workloads.
Configure readiness, liveness and startup probes for their distinct purposes.
Handle `SIGTERM` and shut down gracefully within the termination grace period.
Run multiple replicas, spread them across nodes and zones, and protect them with PodDisruptionBudgets.
Deploy images by a specific version tag or by digest, never `:latest`.
Scale stateless workloads horizontally with the HorizontalPodAutoscaler.
Apply the recommended `app.kubernetes.io/*` labels.
Grant least-privilege RBAC, and give each workload its own service account.
Enforce the Restricted Pod Security Standard for application namespaces.
Start each namespace from a default-deny NetworkPolicy and allow only the traffic you need.
Encrypt Secrets at rest, restrict who can read them, and consider an external secret store.
Decide your tenancy model (namespaces, clusters) explicitly.
Keep all manifests declarative and in Git, and let an agent reconcile the cluster to them (GitOps).
Treat every Server Action as a public endpoint: authenticate, authorize and validate its input inside the action.
Give an environment variable the `NEXT_PUBLIC_` prefix only if its value may be public.
Put data access in a server-only Data Access Layer that checks authorization and returns minimal data transfer objects (DTOs).
Pass Client Components, and return from Server Actions, only the fields the UI renders.
Add `import 'server-only'` to modules that use secrets or the database.
Keep `"use client"` boundaries small: mark the interactive components, not whole layouts or pages, and pass server-rendered content to them as `children` or props.
Decide caching per data source, and invalidate the cache in every mutation that changes the data.
Read data in Server Components and change it with Server Actions.
Avoid request waterfalls: start independent requests in parallel, and stream slow parts behind `<Suspense>` or `loading.js`.
Return expected errors, such as failed validation, from Server Actions as values, and let `error.js` and `global-error.js` boundaries catch uncaught exceptions.
Use `next/image`, `next/font` and `next/script` instead of plain `` tags, font links and script tags.
Don't block the event loop.
Await or return every promise, and don't pass async functions where the caller ignores the returned promise.
Validate all external input, such as request bodies, query strings and messages, at runtime with a schema library.
Commit the lockfile, install with `npm ci`, and check dependencies for known vulnerabilities in CI.
Run only Active LTS or Maintenance LTS releases of Node.js in production.
Treat unknown errors as fatal: log them, shut down gracefully and let the platform restart the process.
Structure the service by business components, each with its own entry points, domain logic and data access, and keep web-framework objects out of the domain logic.
Keep TypeScript's `strict` option on, and type-check in CI with `tsc`.
Shut down gracefully on `SIGTERM`: fail the readiness check, stop accepting connections, finish in-flight requests, close resources, then exit.
Log structured JSON to stdout with a mature logger such as Pino, add request context with child loggers, and redact secrets.
Handle errors in one central handler that every entry point (HTTP routes, jobs, message consumers) calls, and throw only `Error` objects or subclasses of it.
Set HTTP server timeouts and connection limits, and put a reverse proxy in front of the service.
Define SLOs from user-facing SLIs, and use the error budget to balance reliability against release speed.
Monitor the four golden signals for every user-facing service: latency, traffic, errors and saturation.
Put a timeout on every remote call, and retry only with capped exponential backoff and jitter.
Design to prevent cascading failures, for example with load shedding and by avoiding retry storms.
Stop calling a failing dependency with a circuit breaker, and isolate resources with bulkheads.
Avoid fallback paths that are rarely exercised.
Buffer bursts of load with queues between producers and consumers.
Verify resilience with controlled chaos experiments.
Keep config in the environment, treat backing services as attached resources, and run stateless processes.
Expose health endpoints that load balancers and orchestrators can probe.
Instrument with OpenTelemetry and follow its semantic conventions, so telemetry is portable and correlated.
Run blameless postmortems and track their action items.
Spend architecture effort on the decisions that are hard to change.
Treat internal quality as a speed investment, not a cost.
Reduce irreversibility where you can.
Separate concerns and encapsulate decisions behind interfaces.
Gather together the things that change for the same reasons; separate those that change for different reasons.
Point dependencies at abstractions and make them explicit.
Decompose by design decisions likely to change, not by processing steps.
Keep each piece of knowledge in one place (DRY).
Don't build capabilities for presumed future needs (YAGNI), but do keep the code easy to change.
Prefer the simplest design that passes the tests, reveals intention, has no duplication and has the fewest elements.
Take on technical debt deliberately and prudently, and know when you're doing it.
Expect system structure to mirror communication structure (Conway's law).
Aim for an architecture where teams can test and deploy independently.
Shape teams to get the architecture you want (Inverse Conway Maneuver).
Draw team boundaries to manage cognitive load, using clear team types and interaction modes.
Write quality requirements as concrete, measurable scenarios, not adjectives.
Pick the few (three to five) quality goals that drive the design and make the trade-offs between them explicit.
Protect key characteristics with automated architectural fitness functions that run in the delivery pipeline.
When the architecture is a key business asset, evaluate it with stakeholders against prioritised scenarios early, before committing.
Keep components and hooks pure. Side effects belong in event handlers or Effects.
Keep state minimal.
Don't use Effects to transform data or handle user events.
Put state where it's used, and lift it only as far as the closest common parent.
Treat server state (fetched and cached data) separately from UI state, for example with TanStack Query.
Test the way users use the UI, not implementation details.
Start new apps with a framework, or with a build tool such as Vite when you have specific constraints.
Try props and composition before reaching for context.
Extract reusable stateful logic into custom hooks.
Organise larger apps by feature, not by file type.
Move non-view logic (domain, data access) out of components as the app grows.
Track Core Web Vitals as the user-facing performance budget.
Deny by default, enforce least privilege, and check authorisation server-side on every request.
Keep secrets out of code and repositories.
Threat model early and revisit it as the design changes.
Log security-relevant events, and keep secrets and sensitive personal data out of logs by removing, masking, hashing or encrypting them.
Secure service-to-service communication and identity in distributed systems.
Ship secure defaults so customers don't have to harden the product themselves.
Don't grant implicit trust based on network location. Authenticate and authorise every access (zero trust).
Protect the software supply chain with build provenance and continuous dependency health checks.
Use STRIDE to enumerate threats per component, data flow and trust boundary.
Start with a well-structured monolith and split it once the boundaries are understood.
Have rapid provisioning, basic monitoring and rapid deployment in place before adopting microservices.
Organise services around business capabilities and let each service own its data.
Treat microservices as a premium you pay to manage complexity.
Consider a modular monolith: one deployable with strictly enforced module boundaries.
Keep the domain independent of UI, frameworks and databases, so that dependencies point inwards.
Layer presentation, domain and data, but in larger systems make domain modules the top-level split.
Apply CQRS only to the specific parts of a system that need it.
Use event sourcing where a full history of changes is a requirement, not as a default persistence model.
Say which event-driven pattern you mean: event notification, event-carried state transfer, event sourcing or CQRS.
Replace legacy systems incrementally behind a facade (Strangler Fig) rather than with a big-bang rewrite.
Put an anti-corruption layer between your model and legacy or external models.
When extracting services, start with a simple, loosely coupled capability and decouple by business capability, not by technical layer.
Write many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests and very few end-to-end tests.
Keep the software deployable at all times, and prioritise that over new features.
Integrate small changes into the main branch at least daily.
Enforce architecture rules such as layering and dependency direction with automated tests.
Test service boundaries with contract tests rather than relying on slow, brittle end-to-end integration suites.
Decouple deployment from release with feature toggles, and remove toggles once they've served their purpose.
Measure software delivery throughput and instability with the DORA metrics, and use them to improve, not to compare teams.
Store state in a remote backend with locking and encryption at rest, restrict who can read it, and never commit state files.
Give Terraform short-lived credentials, such as OIDC from the CI platform or HCP Terraform dynamic provider credentials, instead of static keys. Never put credentials in provider blocks or variables.
Keep secrets out of state where the provider allows it, with ephemeral values and write-only arguments (Terraform 1.10 and 1.11 or later), and protect saved plan files like state.
Split infrastructure into separate root modules, each with its own state, by environment, blast radius, rate of change and team ownership.
Give each environment its own directory, with its own backend, that calls shared modules. Don't use CLI workspaces for environments that need separate credentials or access controls.
Rename and move resources with `moved` blocks, and keep old `moved` blocks in shared modules.
Keep the module tree flat: compose child modules in the root module and pass their dependencies in as variables.
Write modules that do one thing well at a higher level of abstraction, not thin wrappers around a single resource.
Protect costly stateful resources, such as databases and storage, with `prevent_destroy`, sparingly.
Pin versions: set `required_version`, constrain providers with `~>` in root modules but only by minimum in reusable modules, pin module versions, and commit `.terraform.lock.hcl`.
Run Terraform from a pipeline: plan every change, save the plan with `-out`, and apply exactly that plan after review.
Run `terraform fmt -check`, `terraform validate` and TFLint on every change, and test reusable modules with `terraform test`.
Check plans against security and organisation policies as code before applying them.
Detect drift on a schedule, for example with `terraform plan -detailed-exitcode` or HCP Terraform health assessments.
Keep logic that doesn't need the engine in plain C# classes, with MonoBehaviours as thin adapters.
Separate UI from game logic with Model-View-Presenter (or MVC).
Model complex behaviour, such as characters, AI and game flow, with the State pattern instead of growing `switch` statements.
Wrap player and AI actions in commands when you need undo, replay, rebinding or queuing.
Put designer-tunable, shared data in ScriptableObject assets, not hard-coded values or copies on every prefab.
Don't use ScriptableObjects as save-game storage.
Use ScriptableObject-based enums when designers need to add values without code changes.
Make dependencies explicit through serialized references, constructor or method injection, or a DI container (for example VContainer), rather than singletons and scene-wide `Find` lookups everywhere.
Don't rely on the order in which Unity calls the same event function (`Awake`, `Start`, …) on different objects.
Decouple systems with events.
For asynchronous code, use `Awaitable` with async/await (Unity 2023.1+) or coroutines, and know which thread each continuation runs on.
For multiplayer, choose the netcode stack with the Multiplayer Center and study Boss Room before designing your own architecture.
Choose the UI system (UI Toolkit or uGUI) per use case using Unity's comparison.
Choose the Entities package (DOTS/ECS) deliberately for large simulations.
Profile early and on target devices, and measure before and after every optimisation.
Pair every Addressables load with a release.
Avoid managed allocations in per-frame code paths to prevent garbage-collector spikes.
Keep the `Resources` folder for prototypes and small bootstrap data. Load game content through Addressables (or AssetBundles).
Pool objects that are created and destroyed often, such as projectiles, effects and UI list items, using `UnityEngine.Pool`.
Agree on one folder structure and naming convention, write it down, and keep your own assets separate from third-party assets.
Know Unity's reserved folder names (`Editor`, `Resources`, `StreamingAssets`, `Plugins`, …) and use them only for their purpose.
Agree on a team C# style guide, starting from Unity's example and adapting it. Apply it consistently, and enforce formatting with an EditorConfig file.
Split code into assemblies with Assembly Definition files once the project grows.

Mirror the architecture in assemblies, for example `Game.Core` (no engine-specific dependencies where practical), `Game.Gameplay`, `Game.UI`, `Game.Editor` and `*.Tests`, so that wrong-way references fail to compile.
Move systems that several projects share into custom UPM packages that follow the standard package layout.
Keep `.meta` files visible and committed, and keep asset serialization on Force Text, so that assets diff and merge.
Start from the community Unity `.gitignore` so that generated folders such as `Library/` and `Temp/` are never committed.
Configure UnityYAMLMerge (Smart Merge) as the merge tool for scenes and prefabs.
Enter Play mode without domain reload for faster iteration.
Design for testability: keep logic in plain C# classes behind thin MonoBehaviours, and inject dependencies.
Run the tests from the command line in batch mode as part of the build, so CI runs them on every change.
Write plain NUnit `[Test]` tests in Edit Mode for logic that doesn't need Play mode, and use `[UnityTest]` Play Mode tests for runtime behaviour that spans frames or needs a scene.
Put tests in their own test assemblies that reference the assemblies under test.
